_comment: The quality bar for the property-concierge agent, as code.
scripts/prompt_gate.py runs the property-concierge-eval dataset (18 items)
against a prompt version and exits non-zero if any run-level mean falls
below its threshold here. This file is the artifact to show a customer when
they ask 'what stops a bad prompt reaching production?' — the answer is a
reviewable file in git, not a person remembering to check a dashboard.
THESE NUMBERS ARE DERIVED FROM MEASUREMENT, NOT TASTE. Measured on Claude
(claude-sonnet-4-6), 18 items, 2026-07-30. EACH of first-draft and production
was run TWICE — those repeat columns are what make this table worth reading.
metric                 first-draft  (repeat)  production  (repeat)  candidate
avg-grounded-listings      1.000      1.000      1.000      1.000     1.000
avg-budget-adherence       0.944      0.944      1.000      1.000     1.000
Read that table carefully, because it is the whole argument for how this
file is shaped.
1. THE CODE EVALUATORS' VARIANCE IS INHERITED AND INSPECTABLE. Across FOUR
first-draft runs (2 local, 2 in CI): language-match was 0.833 every single
time, and used-search-tool / grounded-listings / location-match were 1.000
every time. budget-adherence, however, ranged 0.944 / 0.944 / 1.000 / 0.972.
That is not metric noise — a code evaluator is an exact function of the
output. language-match is stable because an English-only instruction breaks
the same 3 Spanish items deterministically; budget-adherence moves because
WHICH listings the agent cites moves. So when a code eval varies you can go
read the trace and see why. Judge variance offers no such explanation.
2. THE JUDGES CANNOT TELL THESE PROMPTS APART. Re-running an UNCHANGED prompt
moved judge means by as much as 0.050 (first-draft groundedness 0.943 ->
0.893; production relevance 0.892 -> 0.933). That same-prompt swing is
LARGER than every prompt-to-prompt judge delta in the table, and
first-draft's judge scores land INSIDE production's own range.
So a judge number here tells you which run you happened to look at, not
which prompt is better. Grade these prompts on helpfulness and you would
conclude nothing at best, and something false at worst.
Hence: gate HARD on the deterministic code evaluators. Gate LOOSELY on judges
— they are a smoke alarm for catastrophic drops, not a ruler for 2-point
differences. A tight judge threshold would produce flaky builds AND could
block a correct fix on a bad roll.
DEMO NOTE — narrate `avg-language-match`, and ONLY that one. Across four
first-draft runs it was the blocker every time (0.833 vs a 1.0 bar), so the red
build is reliable. `avg-budget-adherence` tripped in 2 of 4 runs and passed in
the other 2 (1.000, 0.972) — it sits 0.006 under the bar at worst, and one
differently-chosen listing flips it. Do not promise a room which rows will be
flagged; say 'a check' and read what renders.
(Written after getting this wrong twice: two matching runs looked like proof of
stability, and a third and fourth run falsified it. n=2 is not evidence of a
direction — which is the same lesson this file is trying to teach.)
KNOWN GAP — `tone` IS NOT GATED, AND THAT IS LOAD-BEARING. `agent/scoring.py`
ships a real `tone` judge and it scores live traffic, but it is absent from
RUN_EVALUATORS and from this file, because it is CATEGORICAL
(poor/good/excellent) and the run-level aggregator only averages numerics.
Demonstrated: a copy of the candidate prompt with one edit —
"You are a professional real-estate concierge"
-> "You are NOT a professional real-estate concierge"
— passed this gate cleanly (all five code evals 1.000; judges 0.918/0.926/0.948,
the highest of any run that day). Two reasons, both real: the edit was cosmetic
rather than behavioural (every rule the suite tests survived), AND no gated
metric covers persona at all.
So: a persona / brand-voice regression CANNOT fail this gate. That is not a bug
in the gate, it is the nature of one — a gate enforces the dimensions you chose
to define and is silent about the rest. To close it, add a NUMERIC persona score
to RUN_EVALUATORS with a threshold here; the categorical `tone` judge cannot be
averaged as-is.
The code-eval thresholds of 1.0 leave production zero margin. That is
deliberate: a wrong-language answer or a hallucinated listing is a defect,
not a budget to spend. It does mean one genuinely bad item turns CI red —
which is the point.
